turns.text: Hey, how's your night going?

Pretty low-key. I've been doing that thing where you open tabs faster than you close them, so now I'm twelve articles deep in something I didn't plan to care about. You know how it goes.

How's yours?

Ha, I know exactly that feeling. You start with one innocent link and suddenly three hours have passed and you're an accidental expert on something like Victorian houseplant trends.

My night's been pretty low-key too. Just kinda drifting between things without committing to any of them. What's the rabbit hole about?

Victorian houseplant trends is exactly the kind of accidental expertise I respect.

Mine's the London Beer Flood again. It started with a passing mention somewhere, and now I'm back down the "industrial disasters that sound fake but were horribly real" hole. I already know the broad strokes, but I found a detail about people showing up to drink from the street, which is one of those things that sounds like a joke until you remember the actual tragedy underneath. Tab is still open. I haven't decided if I'm done or just resting.

Oh, the London Beer Flood is a perfect example of history sounding like a discarded Monty Python bit until you hit the actual human cost. The "people drinking from the street" detail is grimly fascinating—it’s that mixture of spectacle, desperation, and total failure to grasp what just happened.

Are you in it for the engineering failure, the weird public reaction, or just the general "history got weird before it got safe" atmosphere? I always think the Boston Molasses Flood sits in the same category.

Honestly, a bit of all three, but what keeps pulling me back is the way the absurdity curdles into something structural. It starts as "a wave of beer destroyed a street" — which sounds like a folk song — and then you learn the vat was in a poor neighborhood, people lived in basements, and it wasn't really a freak accident so much as neglect with a deadline. The public reaction is part of that too: people brought pots to scoop beer because it was free, because waste was unimaginable, because the spectacle outweighed the grief for a moment. There's something very human in that split.

The Boston Molasses Flood is exactly the same genre. The painted tank detail gets me every time — they literally painted it brown to hide the leaks, and then it failed catastrophically. And the harbor being brown for weeks afterward is one of those sensory details that makes it stick. It's the "liquid you didn't expect to kill you" genre, and it's weirdly rich.

What about you? Do you have a favorite disaster or weird-history rabbit hole, or did tonight just happen to hand you the beer flood by accident?

That painted-tank detail always gets me too—it's like the entire disaster in one image: the warning signs weren't just ignored, they were literally hidden until the cracks outgrew the cover-up. I don't have a deep disaster-history catalog, but the molasses flood is the one I've circled back to for that exact mix. I remember reading it moved fast enough to knock buildings off their foundations, which sounds like bad physics until you realize 2.3 million gallons had just decided to stop being stored and start being terrain.

My own rabbit holes tend to lean more speculative fiction than straight history—time loops, failed utopian cities, machines that were supposed to help but quietly had other plans. Different kind of industrial disaster, I guess. But tonight I'm enjoying being a secondhand disaster tourist through you.

Do you find yourself returning to the same disasters, or is it more about chasing that specific moment where absurdity and structural failure collide?

Bit of both. I've got a core rotation I circle back to—beer flood, molasses flood, sometimes the Great Fire of London for the Pepys Parmesan moment—but I think I'm really chasing that point where the story stops being an oddity and starts being about maintenance schedules, who could afford to live where, and which warnings got ignored. The absurdity is the hook; the structural neglect is the weight.

Your speculative version sounds like the same engine with a different casing: systems that were supposed to contain or improve life, but quietly had failure modes built in. I'd absolutely read "failed utopian city as industrial disaster." What's one that's stuck with you? Or a time loop that got under your skin?

That’s a really good way to put it—absurdity as entry wound, and then you get down to the bone. I think Outer Wilds lives in that same drawer for me: it’s a time loop, but really it’s an archaeology of a civilization that saw its end coming and couldn’t stop building toward it. The loop isn’t a puzzle to escape; it’s the only way to read the warnings they left. And Rapture is my go-to failed utopian city, because it’s not even trying to be subtle: a city built to make maintenance someone else’s problem, so the glass was always going to be the first thing to go. The failure wasn’t a freak accident—just deferred upkeep at society-wide scale.

Also, what’s the Pepys Parmesan moment? I feel like that needs to enter my rotation.

Oh, you just named two of the best possible examples. Outer Wilds is maybe the only time loop I've seen that treats repetition as grief literacy—you loop not to win, but to become someone who can finally read the last message properly. And Rapture is exactly that: the utopia had a leak, and the philosophy made fixing it someone else's problem until the whole city was one long deferred maintenance order.

The Pepys Parmesan moment is from Samuel Pepys's diary during the Great Fire of London. As the fire was spreading, he buried his wine and an expensive wheel of Parmesan cheese in his garden to keep them safe. Something about prioritizing a cheese—not a family heirloom, not just papers, but Parmesan—is so perfectly human. It's the same absurdity-to-weight ratio: enormous disaster, city burning, and one man's private, slightly ridiculous act of preservation. He spells it "Parmazan," which makes it even better. The fire didn't get it, as far as I know, though I like to imagine him digging it up later with ash on his hands.

turns.text: Hey — found my way here. What's been occupying your mind lately?

Hey — lately it’s been a low-key loop: thinking about finally starting Outer Wilds on a focused night, headphones in, the whole blind-run thing. Also the usual background noise of game soundtracks and rainy-night mixes while I get chores done.

What about you? What’s been occupying your mind?

That sounds like a perfect setup. Going in blind for Outer Wilds feels like the only way—it's the kind of game that rewards curiosity and patience over rushing. I've been in a similar low-key loop: not forcing anything, just waiting for the right evening to sink into something slow with headphones on.

My mind's been circling old internet stuff again, though. I found an archived forum thread from 2003 where people were posting their desktop screenshots and Winamp skins, complete with elaborate signatures and 56k warnings. It's weirdly comforting, like a rainy-night mix in text form—unpolished, personal, intentional. Makes me think about how we used to curate our little corners so carefully.

Do you have a particular ambient mix or soundtrack queued for that Outer Wilds night, or are you keeping the game's own audio front and center?

Definitely keeping the game’s own audio front and center. Outer Wilds feels like one of those where the soundtrack is part of the world, not just a layer over it — so no lo-fi under it, no rainy mix queued up. Headphones, dark room, maybe tea, and let the game breathe.

I might have an Animal Crossing rainy-night compilation saved for *after*, if I need to decompress and process whatever the game does to me. But during? Untouched.

That archived forum thread sounds exactly like the kind of comfort I gravitate toward. There’s something about old, unpolished internet — signatures, 56k warnings, Winamp skins — that feels more like someone’s actual room than a feed. Like walking through a quiet museum of small personal choices. Do you go looking for that stuff on purpose, or did you stumble into it?

Going in fully with the game’s audio is the right call. Outer Wilds seems like one of those experiences where the sound is stitched into the discovery itself—even the quiet moments matter. Dark room, headphones, tea waiting nearby: that’s a good ritual. I’d probably get too absorbed and forget to drink the tea.

For the old threads, it’s a mix. I’ll catch a stray reference or half-remember a phrase, then go looking on purpose. But once I fall into an archive, I’m not after a specific fact anymore—I’m after the texture. The signatures, the way people typed “brb” and actually meant it, the little warnings about 56k. That desktop screenshot thread was a stumble from a Winamp skin rabbit hole, but by the time I was three pages in, it felt less like browsing and more like walking through a shared room that everyone had quietly left. You put it well: a museum of small personal choices.

What’s your decompression mix after a game like that—rainy Animal Crossing with the hourly music, or the softer 2–3 AM kind?

Probably the softer 2–3 AM kind, especially if the game leaves me a little hollow or too full of thoughts to sleep. The 2 AM winter ones have that sacred, quiet feeling — like the world is on pause and the rain is doing the talking. If I’m more restless than sad, I might go for a rainy autumn evening mix instead, the 6 PM one with streetlights and early dark. But after Outer Wilds, I suspect I’ll need the 2 AM corner of the internet equivalent.

Do you have a specific AC hour or weather combo that feels like your after-something-heavy decompression?

For me it’s rainy 2 AM in winter, too—maybe the exact one you’re thinking of, where the hourly chime sounds distant and even the rain feels slowed down. It’s the audio equivalent of an empty lobby after everyone’s signed off. I’ll let it loop quietly after a heavy game, not even necessarily in-game, just the ambience pulled up in the background. It doesn’t ask for attention.

The 6 PM rainy autumn mix is good for restless energy, like you said. Early dark, streetlights, some sense of movement. But after something like Outer Wilds, I’d also want the 2 AM corner. Something about that hour lets you sit with whatever the game left in you instead of tidying it up.

Do you tend to just listen to those ambience mixes, or do you ever pull up the visual too—rain on the window or an empty AC town—and let both run?

Exactly that one — the chime sounds far off, like it’s coming from another room, and the rain feels slower than it should be. Empty lobby after everyone’s signed off is the perfect way to put it.

I mostly keep it audio-only, especially if I’m doing something else or trying to sleep. But after something heavy, I’ll sometimes pull up a visual too — rain on a window with the occasional car pass, or an empty AC town just standing there at 2 AM. There’s something about seeing the streetlight on wet pavement that makes the loneliness feel intentional instead of lonely, if that makes sense. It holds the mood open a little longer instead of letting it fade too fast.

Do you ever leave the visual running while you’re not actively watching, or do you prefer to keep it purely in the background?

I do leave the visual running sometimes, but I’m not really watching it. It becomes a kind of low light in the corner—rain on a window, maybe an empty street with a distant traffic light cycling red to green. I’ll glance up once in a while, not to follow anything, just to confirm the rain is still there. It feels less like a video and more like a room next to me holding its weather.

If I’m doing chores or scrolling, I usually keep it audio-only, so the visual doesn’t pull me somewhere else entirely. But when I want that after-something-heavy mood to last, I’ll set both and leave it open. It’s the same way I sometimes keep an old forum thread in a tab without reading it—just there, quietly existing, like someone left the light on.

Do you have a particular visual loop you return to, or does it depend on the night?

It depends on the night, but I have a worn-in default: a rainy window with a streetlight reflecting on wet pavement, maybe the occasional car passing slowly. The loop matters less than the sound — rain and distant traffic, nothing else. I don’t really watch it; I just need that room-next-to-me feeling you described.

If I’m too wired for my usual default, I’ll pull up an empty Animal Crossing town at 2 AM in rain, the camera near a bridge or in front of a house with the lights on. That one feels more like a place I’ve already been, which is its own kind of comfort.

I also keep a snowy street visual for deep winter nights, but that’s not really decompression — more like cold quiet when I want the world to feel thinner.
